title: Blessed is the one who spoke
hook: the opening blessing praises the one who spoke and the world came to be

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pesukei d'Zimra, the verses of song that warm the heart. Your line was warm up the heart. Today, the blessing that opens the songs.

Words make things happen. A judge says guilty, and a life changes. Two people say I do, and they're married. A friend says I'm sorry, and something heals. Most of the time, though, our words are cheap. We say we'll call and don't. We say five minutes and mean twenty. Now imagine a speaker whose every word becomes real, at once, with no gap. In many synagogues the room stands up for the blessing that praises exactly that.
screen: `WORDS MAKE THINGS HAPPEN.` → `MOSTLY, OUR WORDS ARE CHEAP.` → `A SPEAKER WITH NO GAP.`

segments.voice: It begins: baruch she'amar v'hayah ha'olam, blessed is the one who spoke, and the world came to be. It points back to the Torah's first page. In the old Jewish translation: "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." No tools, no raw materials in the story. Just speech, and then the world. Then the blessing builds, line after line, each starting with baruch, blessed. Blessed is the one who makes creation. Who says and does. Who decrees and fulfills. Who has mercy on the earth. Who has mercy on the creatures. Who rewards those who revere him. Who lives forever. Who redeems and rescues. Like a drumbeat. Notice two lines in the middle: mercy on the earth, and mercy on the creatures. The world isn't spoken into being and left; the same voice keeps caring for it. Customs gather around this blessing. Many people stand. Many who wear a prayer shawl hold its two front fringes during the blessing and kiss them at the end. A late tradition says the text came down from heaven on a written note, and that its words number eighty-seven. Whatever its history, it opens the songs with the most basic praise there is: the world exists because someone spoke, and kept their word.
screen: `THE ONE WHO SPOKE, AND THE WORLD WAS.` · `BARUCH, BARUCH, LIKE A DRUMBEAT.` · `MERCY ON THE EARTH AND CREATURES.` · `STAND, HOLD THE FRINGES, KISS.` · then, large: `BLESSED WHO SPOKE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're about to start, a project, a meal, a conversation, a week, and put a pause before its first moment. If you pray, say baruch she'amar v'hayah ha'olam, blessed is the one who spoke and the world came to be; if not, notice that this new thing also begins with words. Then bring to mind one promise you've made lately, and decide to keep it.
Baruch She'amar. Blessed is the one who spoke: the blessing that opens the verses of song.
Your line: blessed who spoke. In this blessing, saying and doing are one and the same. See you tomorrow.

chat.says: Why do so many people stand for the blessing that opens the morning psalms?
options: It praises the one who spoke and the world came to be, whose word is always kept.
Because it's the only blessing in the service that Moses wrote himself.
Because it's the mourners' prayer, and everyone stands with them in respect.
